queue.tree_name: The Cucumber Magnolia of Park Oliwski
queue.recognise: A broad crown over a trunk 328 centimetres round by a reader's tape, cucumber-shaped green fruit in late summer; a second cucumber magnolia, 308 centimetres by their measure, stands close by.
queue.story:
Most people picture a magnolia as a garden shrub holding up pink goblets in April. This one is 19 metres tall with a trunk 271 centimetres round.

Magnolia acuminata is a forest tree from eastern North America, and it is called the cucumber tree for its unripe fruit, a knobbly green cylinder a few centimetres long that reddens through late summer. Its flowers are the anticlimax of the genus: greenish yellow, held high in the crown, easy to stand underneath and miss completely. What the species does instead is get big, and this specimen has done it a long way north of anywhere it grows wild.

It went onto Poland's register of natural monuments on 15 March 1992 as number 837, measured then at
queue.name: The Cucumber Magnolia of Park Oliwski

queue.tree_name: The Ivy Elm of Park Oliwski
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the flowering ivy growing up the trunk, which is 420 centimetres round. It stands by the pond in Park Oliwski, not the willow at the Kupaly-Subislawa pond a kilometre away.
queue.story:
Most of Europe's big elms are dead. Dutch elm disease killed them by the tens of millions across the twentieth century, which is why a European white elm with a trunk 420 centimetres round and a crown at 30 metres is now a genuinely rare thing to walk up to. This one stands by the pond in Park Oliwski and has been protected since 1 July 1988, which makes it one of the older entries on Gdansk's register.

queue.name: The Ivy Elm of Park Oliwski

queue.tree_name: The Giant Thuja of Park Oliwski
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the drooping, scale-leaved foliage on a trunk 219 centimetres round, 23 metres tall. It stands in a tight group of four with two yews and a Nootka cypress, all protected under one register number.
queue.story:
Poland protects four trees on this spot as a single object. A western red cedar, two common yews and a Nootka cypress grow within a few metres of one another in the dendrological corner of Park Oliwski, and the register took all of them on 15 March 1992 under one number, 836, rather than four.

The cedar is the one to stand in front of. Its trunk is 219 centimetres round and it carries 23 metres of dense, drooping, scale-leaved foliage; Gdansk's survey of its protected trees singles out the giant thujas of Park Oliwski as one of the collection's standouts, and this is the one that clears two metres of girth. queue.tree_name: The Finer Holm Oak of Edinburgh Gardens
queue.recognise: You can recognise it as an evergreen oak with small dark leaves all year among the park's elms, which are bare in winter, on a trunk about 5.56 metres round. It stands near the bowling club in Edinburgh Gardens.
queue.story: Edinburgh Gardens has two holm oaks, and the National Trust of Australia has a view about which one to look at. Its Significant Tree Register calls this the finer of the two examples of the species in the gardens, and it is certainly the heavier. The City of Yarra records 177 centimetres of diameter at breast height, which is about 5.56 metres of girth, since that 177 is a width across the trunk and not a measurement around it. That is the thickest trunk here and a record nowhere else, since the Trust's own significance statement points to a tree at Talindert, near Camperdown in western Victoria, as the biggest of its kind in Victoria. queue.name: The Finer Holm Oak of Edinburgh Gardens

queue.tree_name: The Three-Trunked Katsura of Park Oliwski
queue.recognise: You can recognise it by the three trunks splitting low out of one tree, 168, 189 and 158 centimetres round, carried up to 25 metres. It stands in the old dendrological corner of Park Oliwski.
queue.story:
In October this tree smells of caramel. Katsura leaves give off a scent as they yellow and fall, variously described as burnt sugar, toffee or gingerbread, strong enough on a still afternoon that people look around for a bakery. It is one of the few trees you can find with your nose.

The rest of the year it is worth finding for its shape. A single katsura here has split into three trunks low down, measuring 168, 189 and 158 centimetres round, and carried all three to 25 metres. Poland registered it as a natural monument on 15 March 1992 under number 838, describing it in Polish as grujecznik japonski trojpienny: the three-trunked Japanese katsura. queue.name: The Three-Trunked Katsura of Park Oliwski
